title: Failure mode exploration and routing intake with Argo Dynamics
summary: Initial reliability & incident-tolerance discovery. Customer runs latency-sensitive inference in EU and US, evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for multi-region failover, SSO/KMS requirements, and desired SLAs. Agreed next steps: security docs, trial Dedicated cluster, and a private-deploy feasibility workshop.
next_steps: Maya to send SOC2 summary, encryption/KMS integration notes, and pricing sheet (Dedicated trial options)
Diego to share sample latency benchmark and routing diagram for multi-region failover
Schedule on-prem feasibility workshop with Tom and Aisha next week
action_items: Maya Chen: email SOC2 + security whitepaper and Dedicated trial options (due: 2025-09-15)
Diego Ramos: produce single-pod latency bench for their 3k RPS target and routing examples (due: 2025-09-16)

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-12 16:00 UTC | Duration: 54 mins | Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Ramos, Nina Patel (Redwood) — Priya Nair, Tom Levin, Aisha Khan, Leo Park (Argo Dynamics)

Summary (auto): Quick intro, high level reliability constraints, current infra, and desired SLA/fallback behaviour. Focus on routing policy, failback, and private deploy constraints.

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood inference, i'll be your AE. Diego and Nina are with me — diego is our systems eng who will dig into the nitty gritty.
00:10 Priya Nair: thanks maya, yep — priya here. we wanted to walk through failure modes, what you offer for multi-region, and how we could keep latency tight if a region degrades.
00:22 Diego Ramos: cool. can you share a bit about traffic patterns? e.g., is it steady, bursty, any regional skew?
00:29 Tom Levin: our traffic is geo-balanced between eu-west and us-east, slightly heavier in eu (about 60%). Peaks around 3k reqs/sec for text generation, many short prompts for our product workflows. latency budget is kinda tight; p50 under 120ms, p95 under 300ms ideally.
00:48 Diego Ramos: okay. that's helpful. are you leaning hosted or self-managed private?
00:53 Priya Nair: we're exploring all three — hosted for speed, dedicated for predictability, private because of compliance for a subset of customers. we need to understand fallback policies between them.
01:05 Maya Chen: right, lots of customers sit in that same spot. important distinction: hosted gives fastest onboarding, but mixing hosted and private requires an explicit routing policy. dedicated sits in the middle — reserved capacity in our cloud region you control, with isolation and SLA.
01:20 Aisha Khan: on compliance, we need SOC2 + encryption at rest and in transit, KMS integration for keys, and SSO with SAML. also data residency for eu customers — logs must not leave eu.
01:34 Maya Chen: understood. we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and bring-your-own-key via KMS for Private and Dedicated. Hosted has customer-controlled logs and segregation options, but for strict residency and KMS we typically recommend Private. note: some hosted customers request region-restricted retention; we can scope that. (slight pause) sorry — that sounded like a mouthful.
01:56 Leo Park: how do you handle failover? if eu region drops, do requests go to us-east and what about latency and cost?
02:05 Diego Ramos: we have routing policies: region-preferred, latency-based, and cost-aware. for graceful degradation you can set a policy to failover to a compatible model variant in another region, or route to a smaller quantized variant to reduce resource strain. latency will of course increase; we can measure expected added RTT and add a circuit-breaker threshold to avoid cascading failures.
02:26 Tom Levin: how deterministic is the failover? we can't have a half-second blip cause wholesale traffic shifts. we need controlled ramping, maybe canary traffic split then full cutover.
02:38 Diego Ramos: absolutely. our rollout engine supports staged ramping and automatic rollback on error rates. you can define thresholds like 5xx rate > 1% triggers rollback, or tail latency spikes for canary endpoints.
02:49 Priya Nair: and we need to define SLA expectations. what do your SLAs cover — availability, latency?
02:56 Maya Chen: for Dedicated we provide uptime SLAs by region, plus incident response targets. Hosted has best-effort published SLOs with status pages; Private is contract-defined since it's customer-managed infra. we also provide runbooks and optional managed-support tiers for Private.
03:13 Aisha Khan: runbooks — we want to review those. also audit logs: immutable logs for admin actions and model rollouts. retention policy needs to be configurable.
03:22 Nina Patel: we can share our ops playbook and audit log schema. retention is configurable per deployment type; for Private we let you use your own log sink (S3/GCS) or SIEM.
03:33 Leo Park: quick question — are KV caches shared across regions or per-region? we don't want cold-start spikes when failing over.
03:40 Diego Ramos: cache is per-inference-cluster; we support prefix caching and a prefix population strategy. for cross-region you can set up warmers or a replicated cache strategy, but that introduces replication cost and complexity. typical pattern: keep short TTLs and warm commonly used keys during rollouts.
03:59 Tom Levin: hmm replication seems heavy. can you do request-level mirroring to warm caches?
04:05 Diego Ramos: yes, you can mirror a fraction of traffic from primary to failover cluster to keep KV warmed, or use synthetic priming requests before cutover. both are supported and we can show examples.
04:18 Priya Nair: okay, let's dig into the worst-case failure scenarios. what happens if a whole region loses GPU capacity but control plane is fine?
04:27 Diego Ramos: two main strategies: 1) route traffic to other regions and optionally route to a quantized or smaller model variant; 2) if you have Dedicated reserved capacity in multiple regions we can split load. our fallback matrix supports per-route fallbacks (model variant, region, or degraded service mode). there is also an option for queued degradation where requests are buffered briefly while capacity scales up — this is dangerous for latency-sensitive apps.
04:52 Priya Nair: buffered queues probably unacceptable for interactive flows. we prefer immediate failover with small degradation versus buffering.
05:01 Maya Chen: noted. also worth considering session affinity: if you have user sessions that rely on KV, failing over a session may lose context. many customers use tokenized context persisted in client or a global KV.
05:18 Aisha Khan: for regulated customers we need to ensure data in-flight during failover doesn't cross borders. is there a way to limit failover only within same legal boundary?
05:27 Diego Ramos: yes — you can configure routing policy to prefer region and only failover within a geography. for EU-only customers you can set policy to failover to another eu region, not to us-east. when no regional capacity exists, you can configure either to block requests or to route with explicit consent.
05:46 Tom Levin: what about observability? we need trace-level insight: per-token latency, model-level cost, and per-route error rates.
05:55 Nina Patel: the Redwood console exposes per-model, per-route dashboards, tokenized cost breakdowns, and traces. you can also stream events to your telemetry backend; we support OTLP and common APMs, though exporter names sometimes vary in docs. (laughs)
06:12 Priya Nair: ok, anything about automated fallbacks for degraded quality? say the model hallucination rate jumps, can you switch models automatically?
06:20 Diego Ramos: yes, you can bind quality metrics — e.g., a regression detector tied to eval prompts can trigger fallback to a different model or a cached answer. that's part of our Optimize tooling and the runtime supports model variant routing. caveat: quality metrics need careful calibration or you'll flip too often.
06:35 Leo Park: earlier you mentioned cost-aware routing. how does that interplay with SLA? we can't sacrifice p95 for cost unless business agrees.
06:43 Maya Chen: cost-aware routing is opt-in and can be layered with policy priorities: you can set priority that SLA trumps cost, but allow cost-aware routing for non-critical traffic or epsilon traffic.
06:53 Priya Nair: let's talk private deployment constraints. we have air-gapped sites for some clients. can Redwood run fully on-prem with no control plane egress?
07:03 Diego Ramos: yes, our Private on-prem package supports air-gapped installs. the control plane can be configured to run in-customer VPC or on-prem; you can opt out of external telemetry. note: certain managed features like Redwood-hosted model catalog sync require periodic artifact transfer; we provide offline model bundle ingestion for air-gapped environments.
07:24 Aisha Khan: and keys? can we bring our KMS/HSM?
07:28 Maya Chen: bring-your-own-key is supported for Dedicated and Private — we integrate with common cloud KMS and on-prem HSMs. we provide key-wrapping options and a documented key rotation process.
07:39 Tom Levin: end-to-end, what's the estimated time to production for a Dedicated trial? say we want a 2-week smoke test with 99.9% uptime target for that cluster.
07:49 Maya Chen: we can provision a Dedicated cluster in a region in about 3 business days typically, or faster for urgent cases. a 2-week trial is doable; Diego will help set the autoscaling policy and benchmark it. SLA for trials is our standard Dedicated SLA but with limited contractual obligations — for production we'd sign the formal commitment.
08:06 Diego Ramos: operationally we'll work through load shapes, provide a benchmark harness and suggested batch/kv config, and help you run a simulated failover.
08:17 Priya Nair: perfect. can you show a sample routing config? even pseudo-yaml would be fine.
08:22 Diego Ramos: sure, i'll follow up with example policies: priority lists (region preferred), fallback sequences (model-quantized->region->blocking), and canary ramp rules.
08:31 Leo Park: on the topic of rollouts: model rollbacks need to be auditable. we must know who triggered a rollout and what prompts/regressions happened.
08:39 Nina Patel: we capture rollout metadata, who initiated it, and tie it to evaluation runs. we can export that to your compliance system.
08:45 Priya Nair: one more on networking: we run strict egress rules and use private peering. does Redwood support VPC peering or private link?
08:54 Maya Chen: yes, for Dedicated and Private we support VPC peering, private link, and site-to-site VPN. Hosted can be configured with private link in select cloud regions. we'll share our network requirements doc — it has IP ranges and ports.
09:07 Tom Levin: good. can you also share incident SLAs? mean time to acknowledge vs time to mitigation for P1 incidents.
09:15 Maya Chen: for enterprise Dedicated customers we do a 15-minute acknowledge and a 4-hour mitigation target for P1s as standard; exact terms are in the contract. Hosted customers use our published status page response SLAs.
09:27 Aisha Khan: will you provide runbooks for common incidents like region overload and cache stampede?
09:33 Diego Ramos: yes, we'll share runbooks. many include step-by-step: throttle inbound, shift routing, pre-warm failover, and how to revert. we'll annotate runbooks with telemetry signals to watch.
09:45 Priya Nair: ok that's helpful. i want to call out two constraints: 1) failover must respect data residency, 2) no user-visible context loss on failover for top-tier customers. can you meet both?
09:57 Diego Ramos: for the first we can confine failover within legal boundaries. for the second, preserving session context requires either replicated KV (costly) or client-side context tokens; we can discuss hybrid approach: replicate critical keys only and TTL short for rest.
10:12 Leo Park: what happens to billing during degradation? if we route to a larger model or cross-region, how is that shown to finance?
10:20 Maya Chen: billing follows actual usage and model variant pricing. console shows per-token cost and per-route cost; we can annotate anomalies in billing reports during incidents. you'll get a CSV export for reconciliation.
10:33 Priya Nair: good. any gotchas when mixing Hosted and Private?
10:38 Diego Ramos: main gotchas: auth tokens, model parity, and egress permissions. models need to be available in both environments or you need a model sync process; also latency on hybrid routing can be higher due to network hops.
10:50 Tom Levin: if we wanted a hybrid for backup only (hosted as fallback), is that supported?
10:55 Maya Chen: yes. we typically recommend Hosted as tertiary fallback, e.g., primary Private -> Dedicated -> Hosted, with explicit consent and data filtering rules to prevent PII crossing boundaries.
11:07 Priya Nair: that's promising. what's the recommended process for certifying a rollout with you? we run a compliance review before production.
11:14 Nina Patel: we'd run a pilot with test data, provide audit artifacts, and host a joint playbook review. plus a security questionnaire and SOC2 docs.
11:21 Priya Nair: ok let's wrap with concrete next steps.
11:24 Maya Chen: action items recap: i'll send SOC2 and network requirements, diego will send benchmark artifacts and routing examples, and we'll set a workshop to scope the Private on-prem feasibility. any objections?
11:34 Tom Levin: none. thanks.
11:37 Aisha Khan: thanks all.
11:40 Maya Chen: great — we'll send the materials today and propose times for the workshop. thanks everyone.
